analysis.one_liner: Makes very large gig companies pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on their independent contractors.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 15 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, the bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, when a company hires you as an independent contractor, nobody pays Social Security or Medicare taxes on that money, so the work builds no federal retirement or health benefits. This bill would force companies with at least $100 million in gross receipts that use at least 10,000 contractors in a year to treat contractor pay like wages for payroll tax purposes — with the company covering both the employer and worker halves of the tax. That would give gig workers real Social Security and Medicare credits for the first time. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig workers who contract with very large platforms — drivers, couriers, and similar contractors — would gain Social Security retirement and Medicare coverage on their platform earnings without paying the employee share themselves, since the company would owe both halves of the roughly 15.3% payroll tax under the bill. Social Security and Medicare, which depend on covered earnings records, would also gain revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig workers with no retirement or Medicare coverage

how_it_helps.text: Large businesses (at least $100 million in gross receipts) that contract with at least 10,000 individuals in a year must treat payments to those contractors the same as wages for payroll tax purposes, with the company paying both the employer and employee halves of the Social Security and Medicare tax by doubling the employer-side rates.
The bill counts contractors under affiliated companies together through standard controlled-group rules, so companies cannot escape the requirement by splitting themselves into smaller entities.
The covered amounts are added to workers' Social Security earnings records, so contractors actually build retirement and Medicare benefits from the work.

analysis.who_pays: The very large companies that rely on independent contractor labor — ride-hailing, delivery, and similar platforms — would owe roughly a 15.3% payroll tax on contractor payments. They could absorb this by cutting contractor pay or rates, raising prices, or using fewer contractors. Independent contractors at smaller companies are unaffected.

drawbacks.text: The tax could land partly on workers anyway: platforms could cut per-trip pay or raise fees to offset the new cost, so a worker's take-home pay could shrink even as their future benefits grow.

The bill raises payroll taxes on contractor pay but leaves workers classified as independent contractors, so they would still lack minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance, and employer health coverage — only Social Security and Medicare would be addressed.
The threshold excludes mid-sized businesses and contractors working for smaller platforms, so coverage would be uneven across the gig economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and on the worker's side: a future Social Security and Medicare benefit paid for by the company rather than the worker, and gig work currently builds neither. The honest costs are that companies may claw some of it back through lower pay or higher prices, and that the bill fixes retirement and health taxes while leaving the rest of the contractor-versus-employee problem untouched. It applies only to the largest players, which limits both its reach and its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, so it died without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on April 15, 2024, with 13 other original Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, which has jurisdiction over payroll taxes; that was the bill's last action.
The bill finished the Congress with 15 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no committee consideration, floor action, or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large gig platforms are better off: they avoided a roughly 15.3% payroll tax on contractor payments, and their contractors still build no Social Security or Medicare coverage from gig work. Ways and Means kept the bill off its agenda, so no member ever had to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large gig platforms and their investors

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith

sides.party_line_note: All 16 supporters — the sponsor and 15 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill then stalled in a Republican-chaired committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Gig platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, and other large contractor-based businesses)
industries.note: The bill would make companies with at least $100 million in receipts and 10,000 or more contractors pay both halves of the roughly 15.3% Social Security and Medicare payroll tax on contractor pay. Their interest in the status quo — paying contractors with no payroll tax and no benefit coverage — runs against the workers' interest in building retirement and Medicare benefits.

industries.industry: Social Security and Medicare trust funds
industries.note: Covered contractor earnings would flow into the payroll tax base, adding revenue to the programs that fund retirement and hospital insurance for everyone.
